- As of 29 August 2026, RSV poses a high risk to infants under one year. article.articleHeadline: Hunting Down the Last Cases of Sleeping Sickness
article.articleSummary: Sleeping sickness, or gambiense human African trypanosomiasis (gHAT), persists in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC), with a couple hundred cases still detected nationwide; 471 cases were reported worldwide in 2025, most in the DRC. EU-backed STROGHAT trials test a radically simpler strategy around acoziborole, a single-dose oral drug with 98.1% efficacy in clinical trials, to accelerate elimination. The approach uses mobile teams to screen villages; anyone with a positive test is treated—three tablets under supervision—while samples are sent for confirmatory lab testing. Historically, dangerous melarsoprol and lab-heavy, lumbar puncture–dependent protocols delayed treatment. Acoziborole is safer, avoiding hospitalization, and could simplify remote delivery. The strategy aims to stop transmission by 2030; since humans are the main reservoir, every infected person must be found and treated to prevent resurgence.

article.articleHeadline: An invasive mosquito is threatening Africa's cities
article.articleSummary: Anopheles stephensi, an invasive malaria-carrying mosquito that thrives in urban settings and is resistant to all chemicals used in spraying, is spreading across Africa faster than anticipated. A genomic analysis of specimens from 10 countries shows Africa populations with resistance to current vector-control tools. The species arrived in Djibouti around 2013, likely on a ship from South Asia, and has branched into three expansion routes: Ethiopia → Kenya; Djibouti → Red Sea → Yemen; and Sudan → Sahel → West Africa. It may move circa 300 miles per year, pushing west to Ghana and south to Lagos and Kinshasa, megacities of ~20 million people, raising year-round malaria risk as transmission becomes less seasonal. Djibouti malaria cases rose from 27 in 2012 to nearly 1,700 in 2013 and over 70,000 by 2020. Niger confirmed the presence in 2024 after field sampling and lab confirmation in Kano.

article.articleHeadline: Similar but Not the Same: The Clinical Side of Differentiating Dengue Fever and Typhus Symptoms in Children
article.articleSummary: Sudden high fever in Indonesian children commonly prompts concern for Dengue Fever (DENV) and Typhoid Fever (Salmonella typhi). Dengue, transmitted by Aedes aegypti, presents with abrupt fever 39–40°C lasting 2–7 days, followed by a critical phase (days 3–5) with abrupt fever drop and risk of plasma leakage. Typhoid fever, acquired via contaminated food/water, shows a staircase fever pattern that rises gradually and worsens at night. Dengue is typified by severe headache behind the eyes, myalgia/arthralgia, nausea, and bleeding signs such as non-blanching petechiae, gum bleeding, or epistaxis. Typhoid features prominent gastrointestinal symptoms: abdominal pain, a foul-coated tongue with a reddened edge, and constipation or diarrhea. Misdiagnosis and delayed management can be fatal; early recognition of distinct clinical patterns is crucial for appropriate first aid in Indonesian children.

article.articleHeadline: H1N1, H3N2 and COVID at once? Why multiple infections are becoming common
article.articleSummary: Reinfection with COVID-19, influenza and H1N1 is possible even after prior exposure, especially for people with comorbidities, undergoing chemotherapy, and pregnant women in India. As of 29 August 2026, experts note antibodies wane over time, and mucosal immunity in the nose and upper airways fades, allowing viruses to re-enter. SARS-CoV-2 continues to evolve, with new variants enabling immune escape; thus prior infection may not protect against infection with newer strains, though protection against severe disease may remain. Memory B and T cells persist, but antibody levels decrease, particularly in nasal mucosa. Antiviral oseltamivir is most effective when started within 48 hours of symptom onset, underscoring early medical advice for high-risk individuals. The discussion references India-based physicians, including Dr Ishwar Gilada in Mumbai and Dr Bobby Bhalotra at Sir Ganga Ram Hospital, highlighting the distinction between infection protection and protection against severe disease, and the role of vaccination.

article.articleHeadline: Severe outbreak of hand, foot, and mouth disease among children in schools in Manipur; what is the contagious disease?
article.articleSummary: HFMD outbreak among children in Manipur, India, with several schools reporting cases as of August 29, 2026. Hand, Foot and Mouth Disease is highly contagious, mainly affecting 2–8 year olds, starting with fever and followed by blisters or ulcers on hands, feet, mouth and between the fingers, sometimes with rash and fatigue. There is no vaccine or specific antiviral; recovery typically occurs in 7–10 days with supportive care. The outbreak coincides with rising dengue and typhoid activity in Manipur, with other skin, fungal, and bacterial infections also reported. Prevention emphasizes hygiene: thorough handwashing, keeping feet dry, regular laundering of clothes, masking for cold symptoms, carrying hand sanitizer, and isolating household members with fever or skin disease. No exact case counts are provided.

article.articleHeadline: Health Department falters during Onam season; district-wide communicable-disease prevention efforts off track, five days' data unavailable | news
article.articleSummary: Alappuzha district in Kerala faces faltering Onam-season communicable-disease prevention as health workers take leave, disrupting district-wide surveillance. Five days of vector-borne disease data have not been released; lower-tier facilities struggle to collect reliable information, and available data have not been uploaded online. Only data up to the 23rd of the month have been published; Onam holidays began on the 25th, with the 24th a working day, yet authorities could not gather figures. The report cites widespread circulation of dengue fever, leprosy, H1N1, influenza, and yellow fever-like illnesses, underscoring the need for daily reporting to enable timely interventions. Data collected via IDSP from primary health centers to district hospitals should be transmitted to state and central health ministries, but reporting delays impede rapid outbreak response and containment planning during a critical public-health window.

article.articleHeadline: With the changing weather, viral fever is rapidly gripping children; doctors say—keep these things in mind.
article.articleSummary: As of 29 August 2026, in Jamshedpur, changing weather (heavy rain followed by sun) is driving a rise in viral infections among children. Viral fever, cold, cough, and sore throat are common; about 50–60 children with fever/viral infections arrive daily at Government Sadar Hospital, according to pediatrician Dr. Kamlesh Kumar Prasad. Symptoms include fever with fatigue, body aches, runny nose, cough, and reduced appetite. After rain, wet clothes and sudden exposure to cold air heighten risk. Prevention emphasizes drying and warming the child, dressing in dry, comfortable clothing, staying hydrated with warm or room-temperature water, and avoiding cold drinks. Diet and hygiene are important: give fresh home-cooked meals, wash fruits/vegetables, provide clean water, and enforce handwashing. Do not start antibiotics or other medicines without medical advice; seek a doctor if fever persists.

article.articleHeadline: A YouTuber crossed the five-kilometer exclusion zone that protects North Sentinel Island and left a Diet Coke can on the beach. The trash was the minor problem: a respiratory infection could threaten an entire village.
article.articleSummary: March 2025, a U.S. YouTuber sailed to North Sentinel Island in an inflatable boat, landed, filmed the beach, and left a coconut and a Diet Coke can before returning to Port Blair; arrested two days later. The episode highlights health risks to Sentinelese, who are medically unstudied because contact would threaten them and their immunity to infections is unknown. Historical epidemics in the Andaman Islands—measles, influenza, syphilis, and tuberculosis—contributed to a demographic collapse of the Great Andamanese. North Sentinel Island, 59.7 square kilometers, is a tribal reserve with a five-kilometer offshore exclusion zone; India’s eyes on, hands off policy patrols the area. The 2025 landing shows barriers are not foolproof and the abandoned can symbolizes intrusion into autonomy and health risk.

triage.notes: 記事は2025年3月の不法侵入事件と、それに伴う北センチネル島民（免疫未研究の孤立部族）への将来的な感染症リスクの懸念を論じたもの。実際の感染症の発生・流行は報告されておらず、過去の歴史的疫病（麻疹・インフルエンザ・梅毒・結核）への言及のみ。現時点で具体的な症例やアウトブレイクの発生は確認できないためDISMISSと判定。

article.articleHeadline: As Climate And Strains Change, H1N1 Demands Stronger Global Action
article.articleSummary: H1N1 remains part of seasonal influenza, circulating with H3N2 and influenza B in India, sixteen years after the 2009 pandemic. It continues to evolve; animal–human spillovers can signal changing characteristics, and surveillance remains essential even when case numbers are not peaking. WHO updates influenza vaccines twice yearly to match circulating strains; for 2025–2026 Northern Hemisphere season, egg-based vaccines target A/Victoria/4897/2022 and cell-/recombinant-based vaccines target A/Wisconsin/67/2022, while for the 2026 Southern Hemisphere season the H1N1 recommendation shifted to A/Missouri/11/2025, with the same strain used for 2026–2027 Northern Hemisphere season. H3N2 underwent more significant changes, including a new dominant subclade. Climate change alters temperature and humidity patterns, potentially shifting regional influenza risk: outbreaks may intensify in tropical regions while weakening in temperate zones. Regular influenza surveillance is crucial to detect introductions and inform vaccine decisions.

article.articleHeadline: WHO's H5N1 Alert Gains Urgency As India Battles Seasonal Flu Surge
article.articleSummary: India faces ongoing avian influenza A(H5N1) concerns amid a seasonal influenza A (H1N1) surge. WHO warns Asia-Pacific to strengthen preparedness as H5N1 continues to circulate among birds, with 11 outbreaks in poultry farms in Kerala causing over 54,000 bird deaths and thousands culled. From 2020–2024 India reported one H5N1 death and two more in 2025; there have been no confirmed human H5N1 cases in 2026 to date. The virus belongs to clade 2.3.2.1a circulating regionally. A 19th Biregional Meeting of National Influenza Centres and Influenza Surveillance (Aug 25–27) emphasized turning surveillance data into rapid public health actions and strengthening lab networks and early-warning systems to monitor animal-to-human spillover. Human infections typically result from direct contact with infected poultry; symptoms include fever, cough, shortness of breath, pneumonia; non-respiratory symptoms such as diarrhea, vomiting, abdominal pain.

article.articleHeadline: COVID-like symptoms in viral fever, concern grows; 28,000 patients reached Dhar District Hospital in 25 days.
article.articleSummary: COVID-like symptoms accompany viral fever in Dhar district, India, with more than 28,000 OPD visits at Dhar District Hospital over 25 days in August, averaging about 1,120 patients daily (roughly 140 per hour during an eight-hour OPD). Most cases involve viral fever, cold, cough, fever, sore throat, body aches and weakness, with some patients progressing to chest and lung complications if not treated promptly. The surge underscores household transmission risks, as close contact in families facilitates spread. Private hospitals in Dhar city also report rising patient loads, signaling a wider seasonal illness burden. Health experts urge seeking medical advice early, eating fresh home-cooked meals, drinking boiled water, and avoiding outside food; avoid self-medication, since early treatment may prevent disease progression.

article.articleHeadline: KMC, Metro Railway Kolkata launch dengue eradication special drive
article.articleSummary: Dengue eradication drive launched in Kolkata by Kolkata Municipal Corporation (KMC) and Metro Railway Kolkata, starting at Esplanade Metro Station and extending to September 3, 2026. Jointly led by KMC Administrator Smita Pandey and Metro Railway Kolkata PCMO Rina Mukherjee; West Bengal Minister Agnimitra Paul attends. The campaign targets water accumulation and littering, with notices under Section 496 of the Municipal Corporation Act (1994) and fines of Rs 200–400 for throwing banned plastic or dirt. Spitting or disposing of dirt triggers fines plus a requirement to clean the site and have the act recorded on camera for social media posting. The drive spans all metro stations and adjacent areas, including South Eastern Railway train car sheds and railway accommodation areas with water accumulation; broader state coordination with Irrigation and Public Works Departments. Officials stress a mass movement beyond government action, continuing through monsoon and beyond until September 3."

article.articleHeadline: 11 inmates test HIV+ at overcrowded Sribhumi jail
article.articleSummary: As of 2026-08-29, 11 inmates tested HIV-positive at Sribhumi District Jail in Silchar, Assam (1 convict and 10 undertrials). The jail is severely overcrowded with 445 prisoners against a 187-capacity, about 238% occupancy. Infections were detected during routine screening under the Prison Intervention Programme for HIV/AIDS by the Assam State AIDS Control Society (ASACS). Most inmates were arrested under the Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances Act. Officials say transmission may be linked to injecting drug use outside the prison; there is no confirmed in-prison transmission. Inmates are under medical supervision and receiving treatment per protocols; those needing specialized care are referred to Silchar Medical College and Hospital or Sribhumi Civil Hospital for additional attention. ASACS teams monitor inmates regularly.

article.articleHeadline: Lumpy skin disease devastates Uttarakhand; 180 cattle affected; vaccination intensified
article.articleSummary: Lumpy skin disease (LSD) continues to affect Uttarakhand, India, with 180 cattle infected across six districts as of August 29, 2026. District counts: Nainital 50, Dehradun 46, Pauri 37, Haridwar 27, Udham Singh Nagar 19, Rudraprayag 1. Twelve samples from Nainital were sent to IVRI, Bareilly; 3 tested positive. Vaccination has been intensified statewide, with block-level veterinarians authorized for limited drug procurement and vaccines reported to be in sufficient supply. No livestock deaths have been reported yet. Inter-district and inter-state cattle movement, along with fairs and exhibitions, remain restricted. Vaccination of roaming stray cattle has begun. Authorities note heightened vigilance in areas bordering Uttar Pradesh due to higher LSD burden there, and the ongoing vaccination drive aims to curb spread.

article.articleHeadline: West Nile virus increasingly prevalent in Europe: What is driving its spread and what is the situation in Serbia.
article.articleSummary: West Nile virus is increasingly prevalent in Europe this season, with the ECDC reporting a fully underway transmission season and a rising number of locally acquired cases. The virus is transmitted by Culex mosquitoes. In Serbia, data from the Institute for Public Health 'Dr Milan Jovanović Batut' show 11 neuroinvasive West Nile fever cases from the season’s start to mid-August, across six districts: Central Banat (3), Belgrade City (2), South Banat (2), South Bačka (2), Šumadija (1), and West Bačka (1). Patients include 7 men and 4 women, with a mean age of 66.2 years. Across Europe, several dozen areas in 10 countries are affected by mid-August, most notably Italy and Greece; neighboring North Macedonia and Romania are affected as well. Climate change—longer hot summers, humidity, and rainfall—plus urban breeding sites sustain mosquito populations and shorten the virus incubation in mosquitoes. Health authorities urge personal protection and elimination of standing water; infections are often mild but about 20% develop fever and some have neurological complications.

article.articleHeadline: Kashmir's Rs 5.63-crore H1N1 lab shut since 2022
article.articleSummary: Kashmir’s high-end H1N1 testing laboratory at Chest Diseases Hospital, Srinagar, built after successive H1N1 waves and reportedly costing about Rs 9.88 crore, has remained non-functional since 2022. No microbiology staff has been allocated to operate it, and officials cite it as under “necessary repairs,” with four years elapsing without action. The idle facility raises concerns over Jammu and Kashmir’s outbreak preparedness and wasted public funds on infrastruture that cannot be used during rising influenza and respiratory infections. Tendering for repairs is expected to commence, but the lab’s utility remains in question. By contrast, an influenza lab at SKIMS (established 2010 with CDC-ICMR collaboration) has evolved into a surveillance and outbreak-investigation hub, underscoring the need for sustained capacity to identify circulating strains and unusual patterns.

article.articleHeadline: M18-China Crimean-Congo Hemorrhagic Fever Virus GP38 Protein Shows Broad
article.articleSummary: Crimean-Congo hemorrhagic fever virus (CCHFV) is geographically widespread across Africa, the Middle East, Asia and southeastern Europe. A study on GP38, derived from the M18-China CCHFV isolate, reports unusually broad immunological recognition by antibodies, highlighting GP38 as a promising target for next-generation diagnostics, antibody therapies, and vaccine design. This finding does not constitute a vaccine or treatment, and the paper does not provide experimental sample sizes or neutralization data. GP38 is produced from the viral glycoprotein precursor and lies outside the main entry glycoproteins, suggesting GP38-directed responses may complement those against surface entry proteins. CCHFV transmission is tick-borne (Hyalomma), with animal-to-human spillover and potential human-to-human spread; clinical outcomes range from mild illness to severe disease with bleeding and multiorgan failure. For diagnostics and vaccines, GP38 could enable broader cross-strain recognition, though cross-reactivity poses challenges.

article.articleHeadline: WHO urges Pacific countries to prepare for bird flu threat
article.articleSummary: WHO urges Pacific countries to prepare for avian influenza A(H5N1) spreading among birds in the Pacific, warning of potential spillover to humans as more Asia-Pacific countries report HPAI A(H5N1) in animals. Detections in Australia and New Zealand underscore the wider Pacific threat. The 19th Bi-regional Meeting of National Influenza Centres and Influenza Surveillance (Aug 25-27) prioritized rapid detection, response readiness, and strengthened One Health coordination linking human, animal, and environmental health. A Rapid Joint One Health Risk Assessment, developed with FAO, UNEP, WOAH, SPC and others, will assess entry risk and needed preparedness. Regional actions highlighted Australia's response, Papua New Guinea's integrated respiratory surveillance initiatives, and Samoa's precautions after wild bird detections in New Zealand; Samoa remains free of H5N1 as of July, with biosecurity and border controls in place. SAT1 affects cattle, pigs, sheep and goats and triggers severe restrictions on animal movement, trade and livestock production. The World Organisation for Animal Health estimates costs to farmers up to $21 billion annually, with smaller economies facing around 1% of GDP losses. For Bulgaria, proximity to Greece and Turkey raises regional risk, though official data show no domestic outbreak. Bulgaria began southern-border checks in March 2026, and hosted the European THRACE program on cross-border animal diseases. FAO calls for rapid regional risk assessment and coordination, noting increased risk from summer pasture movements toward Turkey and the Caucasus. Farmers should strengthen biosecurity, verify animal origin, promptly report suspicions, avoid illicit movements, and use VetIS.

article.articleHeadline: Flood Disaster in the Himalayas: Nepal Fears Health Risk from Decomposing Victims.

Authorities have ordered DNA sampling from recovered remains before burial, and unidentifiable victims will be laid to rest at Devghat, Nepal. Health officials warn that decomposition raises public-health risks. Flooding can contaminate drinking water with sewage, damage latrines, and overwhelm sanitation and water-treatment facilities; camps may lack hygiene. Cholera, caused by Vibrio cholerae, is a common post-disaster illness in such settings and raises concern for potential outbreaks alongside the disaster.

article.articleHeadline: Pulmonary cryptococcosis emerges in diabetic, hypertensive patient without
article.articleSummary: Pulmonary cryptococcosis diagnosed in a 65-year-old man in eastern China with type 2 diabetes mellitus and hypertension but no HIV, organ transplant, or cancer chemotherapy history. He presented with persistent chest pain; chest CT showed left upper-lobe consolidation unresponsive to broad-spectrum antibiotics. Bronchoscopy with bronchoalveolar lavage followed by metagenomic next-generation sequencing of BALF identified Cryptococcus neoformans with 999 sequence reads, confirming fungal pneumonia as the disease driver. C. neoformans is an encapsulated yeast with a glucuronoxylomannan capsule that evades phagocytosis and can disseminate to meninges in the setting of waning cell-mediated immunity. The patient lacked classic immunosuppression, suggesting non-classical risk factors—diabetes and hypertension—may suffice for pulmonary cryptococcosis in some patients. The case highlights mNGS as a rapid, culture-independent diagnostic tool for fungal pneumonia in eastern China as of 2026-08-29.

article.articleHeadline: Back to School Soon: Beware These High-Incidence Infectious Diseases! We'll Guide You to Unlock Health Skills.
article.articleSummary: China’s autumn back-to-school season centers on three high-incidence infectious disease groups: respiratory, gastrointestinal, and vector-borne. Respiratory infections transmitted by droplets include COVID-19, influenza, tuberculosis, varicella, pertussis, measles, rubella, and mumps. Influenza vaccination is highlighted as the most cost-effective prevention; campaigns begin from September, with schools strengthening student health monitoring and parents assisting with routine checks. Gastrointestinal pathogens spread via the fecal-oral route and include hand-foot-mouth disease, norovirus, and rotavirus; control hinges on rigorous hand hygiene in schools and childcare settings. Vector-borne diseases—dengue fever, chikungunya fever, and fever with thrombocytopenia syndrome—are tied to Aedes mosquito activity in late summer and early autumn; dengue has no vaccine or specific treatment, so prevention stresses eliminating standing water, using screens and nets, protective clothing, and repellents. Cross-regional student movement raises importation risk; Guangxi authorities emphasize preventive measures.

article.articleHeadline: A method for protecting against brain-eating amoeba has been revealed.

Most infections occur after swimming in untreated freshwater—ponds or lakes—or in areas with warmer climates. Earlier this week, an eight-year-old girl died in Louisiana after infection from lake water exposure. Naegleria fowleri inhabits warm freshwater lakes, rivers, and inadequately chlorinated pools, predominantly in tropical and subtropical climates, including the southern United States, Thailand, and the Philippines. The amoeba can invade the brain during swimming, causing meningoencephalitis (inflammation of the brain and its coverings).

article.articleHeadline: Best Mosquito Repellents at Chiang Rai Pharmacies for Dengue
article.articleSummary: Dengue risk in Chiang Rai persists daytime via Aedes mosquitoes, with bites peaking morning and late afternoon. Best repellents are available at local pharmacies and retailers (Watsons, Boots, 7-Eleven). Choose products by active ingredient: DEET, picaridin, IR3535, or PMD, and follow label directions. DEET 20–30% offers longer protection; Soffell (~12% DEET) is common but may require earlier reapplication; OFF! Deep Woods and Sketolene may contain 25–30% DEET. Picaridin 20% provides about 8–14 hours and is plastic-friendly; price roughly ฿120–฿280. IR3535 protection is typically shorter. PMD 30% can last 4–6 hours but is not advised for children under 3 years and may irritate sensitive skin. Soffell is a budget option; imported Jungle Formula tends to be pricier. Reapply after swimming or heavy sweating; apply to exposed skin and combine with long sleeves, screens, and covered water containers. Always check the label and local dengue guidance (CDC Thailand guidance).

The program also includes Venezuelan indigenous people in transit. Brazil has conducted mass treatment since the 1990s and aims for pre-elimination with a 2030 target to remove the disease as a public health problem.

article.articleHeadline: Costa Rica expands list of countries for which it will require the yellow fever vaccine.
article.articleSummary: Costa Rica will expand, effective October 1, 2026, its list of destinations requiring yellow fever vaccination for Costa Rican citizens and residents traveling abroad. Bolivia, Ecuador, Paraguay, Trinidad and Tobago, Venezuela, Suriname, Guyana and French Guiana join Colombia, Brazil, Peru and several African nations as risk zones for yellow fever transmission. Travelers to these destinations must have the yellow fever vaccine at least 10 days before departure and carry the International Certificate of Vaccination. The update aims to strengthen preventive measures amid ongoing transmission in tropical Americas and Africa. From August 31, 2026, it will not be enough to check passports, visas, or accommodations alone; travelers must verify vaccination requirements, vaccination status, and the certificate. Yellow fever is a viral illness transmitted by mosquitoes; symptoms include fever, headache, muscle pains, nausea, vomiting, and fatigue, with possible jaundice, hemorrhage, and hepatic or renal complications.

article.articleHeadline: Beyond the statistics, chikungunya sequelae can affect about 3,700 people in Mato Grosso do Sul.
article.articleSummary: Chikungunya outbreak in Mato Grosso do Sul, Brazil, persists into 2026 with significant chronic sequelae. By 29 August 2026, SES-MS reports 12,663 probable cases and 30 deaths in the state this year, with about 12,600 infections so far (roughly 89.5% of 2025’s total of 14,100). A field hospital was set up in a school gym in Dourados to treat confirmed cases, including Indigenous communities. Experts estimate 30–40% of patients may progress from the acute phase (5–14 days, fever and joint pain) to post‑acute (up to 3 months) and chronic (>3 months) arthritis, equating to around 3,700 people with persistent symptoms. Chronic disease brings intense pain, swelling, stiffness in multiple joints, fatigue, reduced function, and potential work incapacity. Long‑term follow‑up data on rheumatology care, rehabilitation demand, and work absences remain limited, hindering full assessment of the outbreak’s burden.

article.articleHeadline: El Niño Effect: Foz warns of the risk of dengue and chikungunya outbreaks - H2FOZ
article.articleSummary: El Niño-driven rainfall and higher temperatures raise Aedes aegypti breeding risk in Foz do Iguaçu, Brazil, prompting dengue and chikungunya alerts. As of the latest epidemiological bulletin (Aug 25), dengue has 3,605 suspected cases with 43 laboratory-confirmed and 3,383 discarded; chikungunya has 282 suspected cases with 4 confirmed; Zika is not reported. Health authorities emphasize continuous surveillance and targeted risk-area mapping (heat maps) to pre-empt outbreaks. Public health measures include inspections, wastewater and water-reservoir upkeep, cleaning of drains, and securing water storage; community participation is essential. Symptoms to watch include sudden high fever, headache, body and joint pains, rash, retro-orbital pain, and GI symptoms. Authorities urge preventive actions even in currently controlled settings and provide reporting channels via app eOuve and phone numbers 156 and (45) 2105-8730.

article.articleHeadline: Diphtheria: What You Need to Know
article.articleSummary: Diphtheria is an acute infectious disease caused by toxin-producing Corynebacterium diphtheriae. In its classic form it presents as a respiratory illness of the upper airways (nose, pharynx, larynx, trachea) and is highly contagious via airborne droplets or direct skin contact. The disease remains endemic in parts of Southeast Asia (India, Indonesia, Philippines, Malaysia, Nepal), Africa, and Brazil, with sporadic European cases in Latvia, the UK, France, Germany and Italy. Incubation is 2–5 days (up to 10). Untreated, it can cause myocarditis with arrhythmias and risk of cardiac arrest, and polyneuritis. Diagnosis combines clinical assessment with laboratory isolation from affected sites; treatment begins immediately with diphtheria antitoxin and antibiotics, plus isolation. Prevention relies on vaccination with diphtheria toxoid, included in Italy's hexavalent vaccine. The basic infant schedule is three doses at 3, 5, and 12 months, with boosters at 6 and 14 years and a 10-year booster thereafter, providing near-total protection.

article.articleHeadline: Justice sets a deadline for the state of Acre to certify Hansen's disease victims.
article.articleSummary: Justice in Acre orders accelerated certification of Hansen's disease victims subjected to compulsory isolation and of children separated from their families due to the policy. The 1st Public Finance Court of Rio Branco partially grants an MPAC action. Certification has existed in law since 2018 but only became regulated in September 2025. The state must publish within 15 days the commission’s composition handling analyses and the beneficiary contact channels. Within 30 days, it must present a plan to clear backlogged requests, prioritizing people aged 80 or more and those with serious illnesses. For cases with sufficient documentation, decisions should be issued within 45 days, with certificates issued to victims or heirs. Delivery of documents cannot be contingent on beneficiaries attending ceremonies. Secretaries of Social Assistance and Human Rights, and Health must comply; noncompliance may incur fines. Certificates may be used as proof in requests for federal indemnization from the Union ordered by the Supreme Federal Court (STF).

article.articleHeadline: After a dog bite, even a small wound may require medical attention because the risk involves not only infection but also evaluation for tetanus and rabies, depending on the circumstances.
article.articleSummary: Dog bites require attention even when small because saliva can introduce bacteria and prompt infection, and tetanus and rabies risk must be assessed. Brazil's Health Ministry advises washing the wound thoroughly with water and soap and seeking medical care after an animal bite. Wash with water and soap, avoid scrubbing or home remedies, and apply gentle pressure for minor bleeding. Do not attempt to capture or kill the dog. Do not close deep wounds with improvised adhesives; keep a clean dressing and limit handling. Rabies decisions depend on depth, location, animal status, and observation feasibility; a healthy dog or cat can be observed for 10 days. Care should not be delayed if vaccine or immunoglobulin is indicated. For tetanus, report vaccination history so providers can decide on a booster. Urgent care (call SAMU 192) is required for heavy bleeding, deep wounds, major trauma, or altered consciousness; otherwise seek prompt evaluation.

article.articleHeadline: Environmental Surveillance will conduct a serological survey following a suspected case of leishmaniasis in Jardim Itamarati.
article.articleSummary: Visceral Leishmaniasis surveillance in Botucatu's Jardim Itamarati (North Region) begins Aug 31, 2026, after a dog tested positive. Environmental Health Surveillance (VAS), with UNESP Veterinary Medicine/Zootechny, will conduct a canine serological survey within about 200 meters of the case to diagnose visceral leishmaniasis and educate residents about transmission and prevention. The effort aims to identify additional infected dogs and inform prevention and control strategies per municipal protocols; similar work is under way in Rubião Júnior. Under Municipal Law 6.921 (June 23, 2026), pet owners may not refuse sample collection. The disease is transmitted by sand flies; vectors thrive in moist, organic-rich environments. Preventive measures include keeping yards clean, avoiding organic debris, maintaining kennels and shelters, regularly collecting animal feces, and using vet-advised dog collars. article.articleHeadline: Feira de Santana City Council has requests to bolster dengue control and inspect a tree in a cemetery.
article.articleSummary: Feira de Santana city council submitted two indications to the municipal executive: one to intensify prevention and control of Aedes aegypti to curb dengue and other diseases transmitted by the mosquito, with emphasis on the rainy season and in neighborhoods where dengue activity has been reported, including Tomba. No specific case counts are provided. The proposal calls for expanded surveillance, home visits by endemic agents and community health workers, and reinforced educational campaigns across media to inform residents about preventing standing water and mosquito breeding. The second indication requests a technical inspection of a tree at Cemitério São João Batista in Mangabeira to assess safety for people and tombs, with potential removal or maintenance depending on findings. Both require executive evaluation; no timelines are defined.

article.articleHeadline: Dengue in Latin America: Julio Croda warns of the expansion of the disease due to climate change.
article.articleSummary: Dengue is expanding across Latin America due to climate change, with Aedes aegypti spreading beyond historic hotspots as temperatures rise and water access worsens. By the third week of August 2026, Colombia reported over 70,452 dengue cases. In Brazil, dengue became the deadliest infectious disease in 2024, with 6,600 deaths, compared with 5,900 for COVID-19 and 6,000 for tuberculosis. Four dengue serotypes circulate; serotypes 1 and 2 have predominated, with serotype 3 now circulating and immunity waning after periods of low transmission. Vaccines aim to cover all four serotypes, but protection against serotype 3 in seronegatives remains uncertain; Brazil has administered over 32 million doses. Wolbachia-infected mosquitoes reduce transmission by roughly 60–70%. The discussion aligned with World Mosquito Day (Aug 20) and International Dengue Awareness Day (Aug 26) at Cartagena.

article.articleHeadline: Summer study trip derailed! Four of a 100-member group bound for Cebu, Philippines, contracted dengue fever and returned to Taiwan.
article.articleSummary: Dengue fever cluster detected in Changhua County, Taiwan, linked to a study trip group of about 100 students who traveled July 31 to Cebu, Philippines for a month of language study. Four Changhua participants and family members tested dengue NS1 positive, deemed confirmed by the Taiwan CDC. The group spans 17 Taiwanese counties; 18 participants from Changhua participated, with some returning early due to illness. Taiwan's public health authorities are tracing contacts and monitoring potential further cases. The incident marks Taiwan's first dengue cluster imported from abroad this year; national totals show 145 dengue cases, including 135 imported and 10 locally transmitted; infection origins are Vietnam (28), Indonesia (27), Maldives (16), with Southeast and South Asia as the main sources. Philippines dengue is endemic; July–October rainy season fosters mosquito breeding. Precautions include anti-mosquito measures and travel medical insurance.

article.articleHeadline: Phú Thọ culled nearly 150 tonnes of pigs after detecting an African swine fever outbreak.
article.articleSummary: African swine fever outbreak detected at a pig farm in Vĩnh An commune, Phú Thọ Province, Vietnam. On August 21, authorities from Phú Thọ's Economic Police identified signs of ASF at a farm owned by Trần Văn K. in Thôn Đình. Laboratory tests confirmed ASF virus in eight samples. To prevent spread, authorities implemented containment and culled 1,859 pigs, weighing about 150 tonnes. The farm owner was instructed to declare the incident and report disease status to local authorities and law enforcement. In addition to outbreak control, Economic Police intensified public outreach, urging farms and residents to observe prevention measures and monitor livestock for abnormal signs. Looking ahead, authorities will continue surveillance, inspect breeding facilities, deter concealment or movement of ill animals, and coordinate with local agencies to curb ASF spread in Phú Thọ.

article.articleHeadline: West Africa: Ebola - Togo-Ghana mobilization
article.articleSummary: Ghana and Togo have launched a bilateral technical working group to strengthen health surveillance and emergency response at the Aflao border. The cross-border mechanism will enable real-time sharing of alerts and information between national health services and improve coordination of interventions in case of a common health threat. Core to the arrangement is a joint Ebola virus disease preparedness and response protocol. The International Organization for Migration (IOM) supports implementation alongside Ghanaian and Togolese authorities, providing equipment and bilingual information materials for border teams to raise awareness among travelers and border communities. Canada funds the initiative, underscoring regional efforts to prevent cross-border spread of Ebola virus disease in West Africa.

article.articleHeadline: Tackling methodological challenges to sharpen infectious disease forecasts
article.articleSummary: Ghana faces a methodological rethink for infectious-disease forecasting. During COVID-19’s recovery period, concurrent Marburg virus and Mpox outbreaks emerged amid rapid urbanization and environmental change that alter transmission dynamics. Authors warn models developed in high-income settings misread LMIC epidemics due to fragmented data across DHIMS, LHIMS, the Births and Deaths Registry, HDSS sites, mortuaries, and SORMAS, plus insurance gaps (only about 54% covered in 2021) complicating validation. Diagnostic constraints include reliance on PCR archived samples, scarce long-term storage, and serology limited by timing windows and cross-reactivity with endemic coronaviruses. As of 7 April 2024, Ghana reported 172,075 COVID-19 cases and 1,462 deaths, but underreporting analyses suggest true deaths could be up to 27.75 times higher. The piece notes three interlocking methodological challenges—highlighting data infrastructure and NPIs evaluation—and calls for a concrete, context-specific roadmap to sharpen forecasts.
